title: Sennacherib's Threat: In Whom Are You Trusting?
summary: In Hezekiah's fourteenth year, Sennacherib king of Assyria captures Judah's fortified cities and sends his officer, the Rabshakeh, with an army from Lachish to Jerusalem. Standing where Isaiah once met King Ahaz, the Rabshakeh mocks Judah's trust in Egypt and in the LORD, then shouts in Hebrew to the people on the wall that no god has ever saved a land from Assyria. The people stay silent as Hezekiah ordered, and his officials return to him with their clothes torn.
story: For thirty-five chapters Isaiah has warned Judah not to trust in Egypt and promised that the LORD would defend Jerusalem from Assyria. Now the crisis arrives in narrative form. Chapters 36 to 39 are the only extended prose narrative in the book, and they serve as a hinge. Chapters 36 and 37 tell how Jerusalem was delivered from Assyria, the climax of the book's first half, and chapters 38 and 39 tell of Hezekiah's illness and the Babylonian envoys, which point ahead to the exile addressed in chapters 40 to 66. The Rabshakeh's question, "In whom are you now trusting," is the book's question put in the enemy's mouth.
historical:
Chapters 36 to 39 closely parallel 2 Kings 18:13-20:19, and a shorter version appears in 2 Chronicles 32. The two main accounts are largely word for word, with some differences. Isaiah leaves out 2 Kings 18:14-16, where Hezekiah admits his rebellion and pays Sennacherib a heavy tribute of silver and gold, even stripping the gold from the temple doors. Kings names three Assyrian officials (the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh), while Isaiah mentions only the Rabshakeh. Isaiah alone includes Hezekiah's psalm in 38:9-20. Most scholars think the Isaiah version was adapted from Kings or from a source both used; some argue the material originated with Isaiah's circle and was taken into Kings.

The campaign itself is one of the best documented events of the Old Testament period. Sennacherib, king of Assyria from 705 to 681 BC, marched west in 701 BC to crush the revolt that Hezekiah and other states had joined. His own annals, preserved on clay prisms, claim that he besieged and captured forty-six of Hezekiah's walled cities, shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage, and received from him a large tribute, including thirty talents of gold, the same figure given in 2 Kings 18:14. The annals do not claim that Jerusalem fell. Lachish (verse 2), Judah's second city, fell after a siege that Sennacherib commemorated in stone reliefs in his palace at Nineveh, now in the British Museum, and archaeologists have excavated the Assyrian siege ramp at the site.

Verse 1's date raises a known difficulty. If Hezekiah's fourteenth year was 701 BC, he began to reign about 715 BC, but 2 Kings 18:1 and 18:9-10 place the fall of Samaria in 722 BC in his sixth year, which would put his accession about 727 BC. Proposed solutions include a period when Hezekiah reigned alongside his father Ahaz, a copying error in one of the numbers, or the suggestion that the fourteenth year originally belonged to the account of his illness (chapter 38), since fifteen added years would give his reign its recorded twenty-nine years. Scholars have not reached agreement.
cultural:
Rabshakeh is an Assyrian title, not a personal name. It has traditionally been understood as "chief cupbearer," though it designated a high official who could act as a field commander and spokesman. He stops at "the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer's Field" (verse 2), the exact spot where Isaiah had met Ahaz a generation earlier and urged him to trust the LORD rather than Assyria (7:3). Jerusalem's water supply was a matter of survival in a siege, and 2 Chronicles 32:2-4 and 30 describe Hezekiah's work to secure it.

The exchange about language in verses 11 to 13 reflects real diplomatic practice. Aramaic was the international language of administration and diplomacy across the Assyrian Empire, known to officials but not to ordinary Judeans. Hezekiah's officials ask the Rabshakeh to use it so that the soldiers on the wall will not understand. He deliberately switches to the local language (literally Judean, which the BSB renders Hebrew) to go over the leaders' heads to the people. His speech is psychological warfare. He offers a comfortable life after deportation (verses 16 and 17), a known Assyrian policy of resettling conquered peoples, and he lists cities whose gods had failed: Hamath and Arpad in Syria, both conquered by Assyria in the eighth century BC, and Samaria itself.
literary: The chapter is built almost entirely around one speech, delivered in two parts. The first (verses 4 to 10) is addressed to Hezekiah's officials and attacks every ground of trust in turn: military strategy, Egypt, and the LORD. It ends with the claim that the LORD himself sent Assyria. The second (verses 13 to 20) is shouted to the people and attacks Hezekiah's credibility, repeating "Do not let Hezekiah" three times. The key word is trust, from a Hebrew root that appears seven times in the chapter. The Rabshakeh is an unwitting preacher of Isaiah's own message: he is right that Egypt is a broken reed, and his question about confidence is exactly the right question. His error comes at the end, where he places the LORD among the gods of Hamath and Arpad. The chapter ends in suspense, with no answer given and the officials in mourning.

outline.t: Sennacherib's invasion and the Rabshakeh at the upper pool
The first speech: in whom are you trusting?
The request to speak Aramaic refused
The second speech to the people on the wall
Silence, torn clothes, and the report to Hezekiah

doctrines.note: The Rabshakeh's speech forces the question of faith into the open: what is the basis of your confidence? The chapter shows that trust in God is tested most sharply when every visible reason for it is gone.

The Assyrian argument treats the LORD as one more local god who will fail like the gods of Hamath and Arpad. The next chapter answers that the LORD is not an idol made by hands but the living God, and this is the error that seals Assyria's defeat.

The Rabshakeh claims the LORD sent him (verse 10). Isaiah had said that Assyria was the rod of God's anger (10:5), but also that it would be judged for its arrogance. God's sovereignty over Assyria does not mean approval of its pride.

words.note: Batach, to trust, to rely on. The root appears seven times in this chapter, along with a related noun in verse 4. It is the theme word of the whole crisis: will Judah rely on Egypt, on its walls, on Hezekiah, or on the LORD? The same verb runs through Hezekiah's story in 2 Kings 18:5, which says he trusted in the LORD.

Natsal, to deliver or rescue. The Rabshakeh uses it again and again in verses 14 to 20, denying that Hezekiah or any god can deliver. His repetition sets up the answer of chapter 37, where the LORD does exactly what the Assyrian said no god could do.

Rabshakeh, a transliterated Assyrian title for a high official. It is not a name. The Assyrian term is usually understood as chief cupbearer, and the office carried major military and diplomatic responsibility.

christ: This chapter does not point to Christ by prediction, but it sets out the question the whole Bible answers: in whom are you trusting? The taunt that God cannot deliver returns at the cross, where onlookers mocked Jesus by saying that he trusted in God, so let God deliver him (Matthew 27:43, echoing Psalm 22:8). Like Hezekiah's officials, Jesus answered his mockers with silence (Mark 15:4-5; 1 Peter 2:23). And as the LORD's rescue of Jerusalem in the next chapter overturns the Rabshakeh's boast, the resurrection overturns the verdict of those who said God had abandoned Jesus. The link is a pattern of trust tested and vindicated, not a prophecy.

hard.q: Is the Rabshakeh right that Hezekiah offended the LORD by removing the high places and altars (verse 7)?
hard.a:
The Rabshakeh's argument is shrewd propaganda. Hezekiah's reform had shut down the local shrines and centralized worship at the Jerusalem temple (2 Kings 18:4, 22), and many ordinary Judeans may have resented losing their local places of worship. From an outsider's point of view, destroying a god's altars looked like an insult to the god. The Rabshakeh uses that suspicion to split the people from their king.

The biblical writers see it the other way. 2 Kings 18:3-6 praises Hezekiah for the reform as an act of faithfulness to the LORD, who had commanded that sacrifice be offered only at the place he chose (Deuteronomy 12). Modern historians debate how extensive the reform was and how archaeology reflects it (for example, the dismantled altar at the shrine of Arad has been connected by some with Hezekiah and dated by others differently). What the chapter shows is the enemy's tactic: twisting obedience into a reason for doubt.

questions: The Rabshakeh asks, "What is the basis of this confidence of yours?" How would you answer that question about your own life?
Hezekiah told the people not to answer the Rabshakeh. When is silence the wisest response to mockery or intimidation?
The Rabshakeh tried to turn Hezekiah's faithfulness into a reason for doubt. How do voices today try to make obedience to God look foolish?
